content.title: Build a 90-day business profitability improvement plan
content.summary: A useful profitability plan turns a few operating problems into measured experiments. Use a 90-day sequence to establish a baseline, test improvements, and keep revenue, margin, cash, and service quality in view.
content.directAnswer: Select a small number of controllable profit drivers, establish a consistent baseline, and assign a manager to each improvement experiment. Review outcomes alongside customer service and cash requirements. Keep hypothetical valuation arithmetic separate from an actual assessment of the business; a better operating result does not guarantee a buyer or a price.
content.metaDescription: Create a practical 90-day profitability plan with baseline measures, accountable experiments, service safeguards, and a clearly hypothetical EBITDA example.
content.primaryQuestion: Build a 90-day business profitability improvement plan?
content.searchIntent: Produce a practical owner decision and evidence checklist about ninety day profitability improvement plan, rather than a general overview.

body.text: Start with a baseline the team can explain

Choose a recent period that reflects the work being improved. Agree on the revenue and cost definitions before comparing results. A change in the way a cost is recorded can look like an improvement even when operations have not changed. Ask the accountant to identify classification or timing issues that could distort the baseline, and keep those caveats alongside the numbers.

Break the problem into drivers the team can influence. Examples include repeat visits caused by missing parts, slow estimate follow-up, unplanned overtime, billing delays, or avoidable purchasing errors. Do not assume that the loudest complaint is the largest opportunity. Look for a recurring pattern that can be observed and tested without disrupting the entire business.

body.title: Owner action checklist
items: Agree on consistent revenue and cost definitions.
Choose a few recurring operating problems with observable causes.
Assign each experiment an owner, measure, safeguard, and review date.
Record additional effort and displaced costs.
Separate actual outcomes from forecasts and valuation illustrations.
Document the process that will maintain a verified improvement.

body.text: Days one through thirty: pick a narrow experiment

Give each experiment a manager, a defined change, an outcome measure, and a review date. For a service business, a useful first test might be a pre-visit parts check for one type of job. Record the extra preparation effort as well as the avoided repeat work. Otherwise a team can shift cost from one department to another and call the result a saving.

Set safeguards before the test begins. Customer service, workmanship, safety, and employee workload should remain visible. A faster job is not a useful gain if it produces complaints or warranty work later. Keep a short exception log and ask the people doing the work what the proposed change makes harder. Their observations help explain the result rather than merely reacting to it.
Days thirty-one through sixty: compare like with like

Review similar work under the old and new processes. Note differences in job type, demand, staffing, or supplier availability. A small operating experiment is not a controlled scientific study, so describe the limits honestly. If the result is unclear, adjust the test rather than presenting an uncertain pattern as proven savings.

Translate the observed change into the business's reporting process with the finance owner. Separate actual recorded outcomes from forecasts of what might happen if the process expands. Keep revenue, margin, and cash distinct. A margin improvement may not immediately change cash when collection timing, inventory, or other obligations are moving in the opposite direction.
Use valuation arithmetic only as an illustration

Consider a purely hypothetical company with annual revenue of $5,000,000. At a 10% EBITDA margin, the arithmetic produces $500,000 of EBITDA. At a 15% margin on the same revenue, it produces $750,000. The difference is $250,000. This simplified example assumes the reported margin change is real and measured consistently; it does not show how a particular company would achieve it.

If an assumed multiple of four times EBITDA is applied to both amounts, the illustrated enterprise values are $2,000,000 and $3,000,000. Four times is an assumption for arithmetic, not a market benchmark, appraisal, or offer. Enterprise value is not the owner's net sale proceeds. Actual valuation and proceeds depend on facts and professional judgment outside this example. Discuss the assumptions with an appropriately qualified professional before applying this illustration to an actual decision.
Days sixty-one through ninety: keep what works

Expand a successful change gradually and confirm that the result persists. Write down the revised process, name the person who maintains it, and decide which warning signs would trigger another review. Stop experiments that shift problems elsewhere or cannot be supported by evidence. A short list of reliable improvements is more valuable than a long project list that nobody can reconcile to operating results.

End the period with a bridge from the baseline to the current result, including unfavorable movements and unresolved questions. Explain which outcomes were observed, which remain estimated, and what the team will test next. This framework is intended to improve decision quality. It does not promise a particular margin, a valuation increase, or a transaction outcome.

body.title: A controlled next step
body.text: Hypothetical operating example: a plumbing team tests a parts-readiness check on one repeatable job category. The manager tracks preparation time, repeat visits, and customer complaints. Some visits improve, but the team also finds a supplier delay the checklist cannot solve. The next test separates those causes. The example describes an improvement method and makes no claim about typical savings or results.
